sections.label: Penal Code review timing
sections.summary: The Penal Code was last reviewed end-to-end in 2007.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: The last time the Penal Code was reviewed end-to-end was in 2007.

sections.label: Committee review report
sections.summary: The committee took two years, submitting a nearly 500-page report with 169 recommendations on 31 August 2018.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: The committee took two years to complete this extensive review.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: It submitted a report of nearly 500 pages and 169 recommendations on 31 August 2018.

sections.label: Rape definition expansion
sections.summary: The Bill will expand the definition of rape to include penile penetration of the anus and mouth.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: The Bill will expand the definition of rape to include penile penetration of the anus and mouth.

sections.label: Marital rape criminalised
sections.summary: The Bill will criminalise marital rape without exception.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: The Bill will criminalise marital rape without exception.

sections.label: Abetment causing hurt punishment
sections.summary: If hurt is caused to the minor or person lacking mental capacity during abetment, the maximum punishment is life imprisonment or up to 20 years.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: If hurt is caused to the minor or the person who lacks mental capacity in the course of the abetment, the maximum punishment is imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term which may extend to 20 years.

sections.label: Intoxication defence and MACR
sections.summary: The accused must prove on the balance of probabilities he was too intoxicated to form the fault element; MACR rises from seven to 10 years.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: This includes the requirement for the accused person to prove on the balance of probabilities that he was so intoxicated that he did not form the requisite fault element for the offence.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: We will increase the minimum age of criminal responsibility, known as MACR, from seven to 10 years old.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Children who are below MACR, and those above the MACR but below 12 years of age, who are unable to understand the nature and consequences of their conduct, cannot be held criminally responsible for any act or omission which would otherwise be an offence.

sections.label: Singapore Courts jurisdiction over offences
sections.summary: Singapore Courts will have jurisdiction over offences in this Schedule where any relevant act occurs in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Singapore Courts will have jurisdiction over offences in this Schedule, where any relevant act of the offence occurs in Singapore.

sections.label: Two types of fraud
sections.summary: The first is fraud directly in connection with written or oral contracts for goods and services, and the second is other types of fraud.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: The first, fraud directly in connection with written or oral contracts for goods and services, and the second, other types of fraud.

sections.label: Review of MMS offences
sections.summary: It is timely to review all offences attracting MMS, and MMS is retained for Penal Code, Misuse of Drugs Act and illegal moneylending offences.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: It is, therefore, timely to review all the offences which attract MMS today.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: We have decided to retain MMS for offences in the Penal Code, Misuse of Drugs Act and illegal moneylending offences.

sections.label: Presumptive minimum sentences for eight offences
sections.summary: Presumptive minimum sentences will be introduced for the remaining eight offences as set out in the Bill.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Presumptive minimum sentences will be introduced for the remaining eight offences as set out in the Bill.

sections.label: Provisions coming into force in 2020
sections.summary: Almost all the provisions will come into force early next year in 2020.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Almost all the provisions will come into force early next year in 2020.

sections.label: Enhanced penalties for vulnerable victims
sections.summary: Penalties for all Penal Code offences against children below 14, vulnerable persons due to mental or physical disabilities, and domestic workers will be enhanced up to twice the maximum penalties.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The first category of vulnerable victims are children below 14 years old; second, vulnerable persons due to mental or physical disabilities; and third, domestic workers.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Penalties for all offences in the Penal Code committed against these vulnerable victims will be enhanced, up to twice the maximum penalties prescribed for these offences.

sections.label: Arrestable offences against vulnerable victims
sections.summary: All Penal Code offences against vulnerable victims will be arrestable, even if the underlying offence is not.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: All Penal Code offences committed against such vulnerable victims will be made arrestable, regardless of whether the underlying offence is itself arrestable.

sections.label: Double penalties for intimate partner offences
sections.summary: Offenders committing specific offences against intimate partners or close relations face twice the maximum prescribed penalties.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: If the offender commits specific offences like rape, wrongful confinement, causing hurt, against intimate partners or those in a close relationship, the offender will be subject to twice the maximum penalties that are normally prescribed for such offences.

sections.label: Offences covering duty of care
sections.summary: The first two offences, causing death by sustained abuse and failure to protect, cover persons owing victims a duty of care.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The first two offences – "causing death by sustained abuse" and "failure to protect" – will cover persons who owe these victims a duty of care.

sections.label: Causing or allowing vulnerable victim death
sections.summary: The third new offence is causing or allowing the death of a vulnerable victim.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The third new offence is "causing or allowing the death of a vulnerable victim".

sections.label: Court considers accused persons' abuse experiences
sections.summary: The Bill's clauses require the Court to consider accused persons' past or present experiences of abuse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The clauses in the Bill require the Court to consider past or present experiences of those of the accused persons of abuse as well.

sections.label: Consensual nude images from 15-year-old
sections.summary: Currently, asking for and receiving nude images by consent from a 15-year-old is not an offence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Currently – and some Members might find this surprising when they think about it – asking for and receiving nude images by consent from a 15-year-old is not an offence today.

sections.label: Sexual exploitation of minors
sections.summary: Introduces offences for sexual exploitation of minors aged 16 to below 18, and enhances penalties for trust relationships with minors below 16.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In such cases, the young person's consent – and we are talking about 16 to 18 years – is, in my view, compromised.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We are, therefore, introducing offences involving sexual exploitation of minors of age 16 or above but below 18 where sexual penetration is involved, where sexual grooming is involved, and where sexual communications are involved.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: For sexual exploitation offences by persons in relationships of trust with minors who are below 16 years of age, we will enhance the existing penalties, and we will peg them to those for non-consensual sexual penetration.

sections.label: Lowering sexual grooming threshold
sections.summary: Lowers the sexual grooming offence threshold by reducing required prior conduct from two instances to one and the offender age floor from 21 to 18.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We are seeking to lower the threshold for the current offence of sexual grooming.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We are reducing the required instances of prior conduct from two to one, and we will lower the age floor of the offender from 21 to 18 – clauses 116 and 117.

sections.label: Extraterritorial child abuse material offences
sections.summary: Makes the offences of using or procuring a child for child abuse material, and producing child abuse material, extraterritorial.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The offences of using or procuring a child for child abuse material, and production of child abuse material, these will be made extraterritorial.

sections.label: Child sex-doll offences and penalties
sections.summary: Increases maximum punishment from three months to two years' imprisonment and introduces a new offence criminalising possession, distribution, importation and production of child sex-dolls.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The maximum punishment is sought to be increased from three months to two years of imprisonment.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: And a new offence criminalising possession, distribution, importation, production of child sex-dolls will also be introduced.

sections.label: Voyeuristic recordings maximum imprisonment
sections.summary: Proposes maximum imprisonment of two years for observance, possession and making of voyeuristic recordings if the Bill passes.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The proposed maximum imprisonment terms for the observance, possession and making of such "voyeuristic recordings" are now going to be two years if the Bill gets passed.

sections.label: Maximum penalty for offence
sections.summary: States the maximum penalty for this offence would be imprisonment of up to five years, with the option of fine and caning.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The maximum penalty for this offence would be imprisonment of up to five years, with the option of fine and caning.

sections.label: Condom removal and STD deception
sections.summary: Two types of deception are identified as compromising consent: secretly removing a condom and misleading a partner about sexually transmitted diseases.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In some countries, cases have emerged of men agreeing to use a condom but secretly removing it before or during sex.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In these cases, the quality of the consent provided by the victim would be compromised by the deception.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We have identified, and also if men, usually men, mislead their partner on their sexually transmitted diseases, that is also covered.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We have identified these two types of deception because they carry serious risks to the victim and represent a greater violation of the victims’ sexual autonomy.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We will continue to assess whether there is a need to expand this offence to cover other circumstances in the future relating to consent.

sections.label: Sustained abuse causing death
sections.summary: Clause 83 introduces offences to address situations where sustained abuse and neglect cause the death of a vulnerable victim.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Clause 83 introduces offences which improve the law's capability to address situations where sustained abuse and neglect result in the unfortunate death of a vulnerable victim.

sections.label: Joshua Robinson obscene films case
sections.summary: In 2015 Joshua Robinson was found with 5,902 obscene films, 321 containing child pornography, and many Singaporeans found his four-year sentence inadequate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In 2015, the case of Joshua Robinson surfaced.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: He was found to have in his possession 5,902 obscene films, 321 of them containing child pornography, featuring children as young as two years old.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Many Singaporeans raised concerns that the sentence of four years' imprisonment was inadequate.

sections.label: Presumptive minimum sentence flexibility
sections.summary: Proposed section 303A lets the Court impose less than the presumptive minimum sentence if exceptional circumstances make it unjust for a first-time offender.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The proposed section 303A of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) in clause 169 introduces more flexibility in sentencing by allowing the Court to impose a sentence less than the presumptive minimum sentence if exceptional circumstances made it unjust to impose a first-time offender with the presumptive minimum sentence.

sections.label: Section 409 criminal breach of trust
sections.summary: The Court of Appeal held in 2018 that section 409 on criminal breach of trust by an agent does not cover key charity officers and society officers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: An example of what could be done for a Penal Code provision is by introducing a Schedule for section 409 of the Penal Code.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: It was held by the Singapore Court of Appeal in the 2018 case of Public Prosecutor v Lam Leng Hung, Kong Hee and Others that the provision contained in section 409 on criminal breach of trust (CBT) by an agent does not cover key officers of a charity and officers of a society.

sections.label: Repeal of attempted suicide offence
sections.summary: Clause 89 repeals section 309, the offence of attempted suicide.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Clause 89 repeals section 309, the offence of attempted suicide.

sections.label: Retaining provision saves lives
sections.summary: Retaining the provision is described as more compassionate, will save more lives, and prevents euthanasia from reaching Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In a way, retaining it is the more compassionate approach because, in my view, preserving the provision will save more lives.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Retention of the provision has a further advantage.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: It prevents euthanasia from making its way to our shores.

sections.label: Risk of more suicides
sections.summary: There is a risk that the number of suicides will increase if there is no provision to deter the act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Because there is a risk that the number of suicides will increase if there is no provision to deter the act.

sections.label: Mandatory reporting of suicide attempts
sections.summary: The speaker's fifth reason is that suicide attempts should be mandatorily reported, yet the Bill removes that requirement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: My fifth reason, there should be mandatory reporting of suicide attempts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Yet, this Bill removes the requirement for mandatory reporting.

sections.label: Study suicides after repeal
sections.summary: If the Ministry proceeds with the repeal, the speaker asks that a detailed study of the number of suicides following the repeal be undertaken.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: If the Ministry wishes to proceed with the repeal, then I ask that a detailed study of the number of suicides following the repeal be undertaken.

sections.label: Singaporean Internet users in 2018
sections.summary: As of 2018, 84% or 4.83 million Singaporeans are Internet users.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As of 2018, 84% or 4.83 million Singaporeans are now Internet users.

sections.label: Police reports of upskirt crimes
sections.summary: A 2018 Channel NewsAsia report stated an annual average of 100 Police reports of upskirt crimes since 2013 and over 500 insult of modesty cases since 2015.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A Channel NewsAsia report in 2018 stated that there had been an average of 100 Police reports of upskirt crimes that have been filed annually since 2013, and more than 500 cases of insult of modesty since 2015 which include the use of spy cameras.

sections.label: Harsher punishment for clip offences
sections.summary: The amendment makes recording, distributing and possessing such clips punishable more harshly, matching the hurt and distress caused to victims.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With the new amendment, the recording, distribution and possession of such clips will result in harsher punishment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This will be commensurate with the hurt and distress caused to these victims, ensuring that Singaporeans are better protected against these emerging crime trends.

sections.label: Bill from PCRC and feedback
sections.summary: The Bill is the culmination of PCRC's work, refined by public feedback.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Bill today is the culmination of the work of PCRC, as refined by public feedback.

sections.label: Law updated for online crimes
sections.summary: The Bill updates the law for new and emerging crimes, broadening theft and cheating offences to cover online fund transfers and false information keyed into machines.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, the Bill updates the law to handle new and emerging crimes, such as online crimes, for example, the offences of theft and cheating are to be broadened to cover theft by online fund transfers and keying in false information into machines to generate potentially harmful outcomes.

sections.label: Marital rape immunity removed
sections.summary: The marital rape immunity will be removed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Fourthly, the marital rape immunity will be removed.

sections.label: VCH cases reported to Police
sections.summary: A 2014 Parliamentary Question on VCH revealed about 10,000 cases reported to the Police a year.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: When I last filed a Parliamentary Question in 2014 on the incidence of VCH, it was revealed that the cases reported to the Police amounted to about 10,000 cases a year.

sections.label: Double punishment for vulnerable victims
sections.summary: Sections 73, 74A and new sections 74B to E allow twice the maximum punishment where the victim is in a vulnerable group, unless the offender proves the victim could protect himself or herself like an ordinary person.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Such extra protection is found in the amendments to the Penal Code at sections 73 and 74A and the new sections 74B to E.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: These sections prescribe that where a victim belongs to one of these vulnerable groups, the offender could be sentenced to twice the maximum punishment applicable to the offence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, this potential exposure to twice the maximum punishment is subject to a caveat: that if the offender can prove that the victim was capable of protecting herself or himself in the same way as an ordinary person, then the exposure to double punishment would not apply.

sections.label: Young person age cut-off
sections.summary: MHA is asked whether its CYPA changes will take effect when MSF raises the young person cut-off from 16 to 18 years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Under the current CYPA, the definition of “young person” has a cut-off of 16 years, but the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) has announced that it will raise the cut-off age for protection of young persons from 16 years to 18 years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Can MHA clarify whether the changes it is making to the CYPA under this Bill will be brought into effect at the same time that the definition of “young person” is raised to 18 by MSF?

sections.label: Misuse of Drugs Act example
sections.summary: The speaker says he used the Misuse of Drugs Act as an example of a flexible regime for new drugs, and asks about broad provisions like CBT.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Actually, if Ms Sylvia Lim had listened to my speech carefully, I had actually used the Misuse of Drugs Act as an example of a situation where, if there are new threats, that is, new drugs in the forms of, for example, new psychoactive substances that have hitherto not been deemed as illicit under the Misuse of Drugs Act, then to include that in the Schedule and to say that thereafter the consumption of those types of drugs would be illicit would make for a much more flexible regime.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: So, I am suggesting that if there are broad categories of provisions – I used CBT as an example, CBT is actually 406 but it can be read with 409 – if you look at that, the broad context of it, is it sufficiently broad as a primary legislation to encompass different permutations in subsidiary legislation?

sections.label: Schedules for future threats
sections.summary: The speaker suggests using a drug-classification-style Schedule as an example for developing the Penal Code, without giving the Minister free rein.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Actually, that is not what I am suggesting.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: I am suggesting a situation where, if you look at other threats that we are facing and one threat is drugs, that the threats morph, that the threats can change in future and, if we have a Schedule, as we do in the Misuse of Drugs Act or classification of drugs that makes a certain type of drug which has yet been concocted and has harm as being illicit to consume, then I think that is a valuable example or a valuable way of looking at whether we can develop our own criminal law in the form of the Penal Code to explore such an avenue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: I am not advocating a free rein of the Minister to make, willy-nilly, new offences without coming to Parliament.

sections.label: Stronger penalties for deterrence
sections.summary: The proposed stronger penalties will strengthen deterrence measures against criminals who prey on vulnerable individuals.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The stronger penalties proposed will strengthen deterrence measures against criminals who prey on vulnerable individuals.

sections.label: Maid abuse case convictions
sections.summary: In February, a couple in a high-profile maid abuse case were convicted and jailed, the woman for three years.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Just recently, in February, a couple involved in a high-profile maid abuse case were convicted and jailed.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It was three years for the woman for a number of terrible deeds, including forcing the maid to drink water mixed with floor cleaner and making her pour hot water on herself.

sections.label: SACC childhood sexual abuse report
sections.summary: A 2017 SACC report found that in 90% of childhood or adolescent sexual abuse cases, perpetrators were family members or known to survivors.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: A report in 2017 by the Sexual Assault Care Centre (SACC), the only specialised centre in Singapore serving sexual assault survivors, revealed that in 90% of the cases received on sexual abuse suffered during childhood or adolescence, the perpetrators were family members or were known to the survivors.

sections.label: Voyeurism outlawed by Bill
sections.summary: The Bill specifically outlaws voyeurism and the making, distributing and possessing of voyeuristic images and videos.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Recently, the issue of peeping toms is being covered in the media.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I am glad to see that the Bill specifically outlaws voyeurism and the making, distributing, possessing and distributing of voyeuristic images and videos.

sections.label: Counselling, sex offenders, filming punishments
sections.summary: The speaker asks about counsellors probing domestic abuse, punishing and counselling parents, and enhanced punishments for illegal filming, and asks Police to review conditional warnings.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: For example, when somebody calls a counselling hotline and say that a family member is addicted to gambling, or there is a family dispute at home, can the counsellor proactively ask them if there is domestic abuse involved?

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Further, we should punish and counsel parents who allow their children to come into contact with sex offenders, as well as parents who are aware that their children have been sexually assaulted but choose not to report to the Police.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Under this Bill, punishment for illegally filming others, distributing and watching such videos have been enhanced.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I would also like to ask the Police to review the practice of issuing conditional warning and to look into whether such a practice allows offenders to re-offend.

sections.label: Enhanced penalties and marital rape immunity
sections.summary: The speaker lists enhanced punishments, abolishment of marital rape immunity, and decriminalisation of suicide, and questions subsection 73(2) of clause 15.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, enhanced punishments; second, the abolishment of marital rape immunity and changes in the definition of rape and consent; and third, the decriminalisation of suicide.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I wish to commend the Government on its acceptance of the Penal Code Review Committee's recommendations relating to the extension of enhanced penalties for offences committed against the vulnerable amongst us, namely, domestic helpers, vulnerable persons, persons below 14 years of age, victims in intimate relationships and victims in close relationships.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However, Mr Speaker, I am confounded by the incongruence between the policy basis underlying the enhanced penalty regime acknowledging an inherent power asymmetry versus the newly proposed subsection 73(2) in clause 15.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This subsection renders the section setting out enhanced punishments inapplicable where the accused person is able to prove that his/her relationship with the victim did not adversely affect the victim's ability to protect themselves from harm.

sections.label: Employer exception to enhanced punishments
sections.summary: The speaker imagines an abusive employer citing subsection 73(2) and urges illustrations to clarify the new provision's scope.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is not difficult to imagine a similarly abusive employer, in an attempt to avoid being sentenced with enhanced punishments, citing the exception provided in the proposed subsection 73(2) and claiming that the mere fact of employment did not adversely affect the domestic helper's ability to raise her arm to stop the punching.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I, therefore, urge the Ministry that the abovementioned sections be supplemented with illustrations to clarify the scope and limits of the new provision, if the provision is not omitted altogether.

sections.label: Definition of consent in laws
sections.summary: The speaker notes an informational gap in the definition of consent and urges a clear and positive definition for judicial review and public education.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For a start, there is an immense informational gap in the definition of "consent" in our laws versus the laypersons' understanding of the same.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I strongly urge for a clear and positive definition of consent for the purposes of judicial review and public education.

sections.label: Rising suicide statistics
sections.summary: The speaker cites rising statistics, including a more than 500% increase in children aged five to nine calling the Samaritans hotline, and suicide as leading cause of death for ages 10 to 29.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Because these escalating statistics across all ages of our population are telling us we must: children aged five to nine calling the Samaritans of Singapore hotline increased by more than 500% in less than three years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Suicide is the leading cause of death for those aged 10 to 29.

sections.label: Mental illness and suicides
sections.summary: Research shows mental illness is associated with 62% of all suicides in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Research has shown that mental illness is associated with 62% of all suicides in Singapore.

sections.label: Decriminalising suicide and post-decriminalisation strategy
sections.summary: The speaker notes low prosecution rates for attempted suicide, supports repealing section 309, but wants a clear post-decriminalisation strategy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In addition, we know that only 0.6% of reported cases of attempted suicide resulted in prosecution each year between 2013 and 2015 which, I surmise, at least in recent years, our Police officers have been taking a compassionate approach in practice anyway, despite suicide being a crime.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The repeal of section 309 to decriminalise suicide most definitely helps to destigmatise suicide.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However, I am concerned that this repeal is not supported with a clear post-decriminalisation strategy, including enhanced psychosocial first-aid training for the Police and Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) officers; coordination between the Police, SCDF, the Institute of Mental Health and support agencies, including tracking and monitoring of suicide attempts and support structures, to course-correct should suicides go up after decriminalisation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With the rising number of suicides with our young and our elderly, decriminalisation of suicide must not be done without reviewing and rebuilding our systemic response towards suicide attempts.

sections.label: Ageing, digital future and section 377A
sections.summary: The speaker says ageing and a digital-dominant future will raise these numbers, and calls for doing more for minority groups stigmatised by laws such as 377A, while supporting the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The latter is likely to rise with our ageing population whilst the former is also predicted to escalate with the unrelenting pace of a fast-changing digital-dominant future.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However, we can and must continue to do more for other minority groups that are still stigmatised by our laws, such as 377A, because, through history, we have never made or changed laws only for the majority within our society, including this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding the above clarifications, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

sections.label: Voyeuristic still images gap
sections.summary: The speaker notes the absence of provisions on possessing voyeuristic still images and welcomes new provisions to prevent and deter voyeurism.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: An obvious lacuna is the absence of any provision to deal with the possession of voyeuristic still images, that is, not films nor videos.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: I, therefore, welcome the new provisions to tackle and overcome these pitfalls to better prevent and deter voyeurism.

sections.label: Expunging offending images or recordings
sections.summary: The speaker suggests empowering Courts to order expunging of offending images or recordings when meting out punishments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: One suggestion could be to empower the Courts to simultaneously make an order for the expunging of offending images or recordings when meting out punishments to the perpetrator.

sections.label: Child abuse material provisions
sections.summary: The speaker describes harm to children in child abuse material and supports new provisions criminalising such activities, including for minors aged 16 to below 18 under section 377BL.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Children used in the production and distribution of child abuse material suffer horrific immediate physical injuries as well as emotional, mental and psychological disorders with long-lasting repercussions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: I, therefore, support the new provisions criminalising activities relating to child abuse material and which define very clearly offences relating to child abuse material.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The new provisions have addressed the lacuna in the law concerning minors of or above 16 but below 18 years of age.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: It is now an offence when a perpetrator uses or procures minors in this age group for the production, distribution or sale and possession of child abuse material under section 377BL.

sections.label: Mandatory rehabilitation and offender monitoring
sections.summary: The passage proposes mandatory rehabilitation, therapy and monitoring for perpetrators, continuing after release if a psychiatrist assesses it as necessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Rehabilitation and therapy, including psychiatric treatment or psychological counselling, could be made mandatory which should continue after the perpetrator’s release from prison, if assessed by a psychiatrist to be necessary for the perpetrator’s complete recovery.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Serial offenders could be monitored either by regulators or their counsellors for a period assessed by their counsellors to be necessary and for a holistic approach towards rehabilitating such perpetrators, mandatory regular reporting to their counsellors could be directed.

sections.label: Private security officers as public servants
sections.summary: The member asks whether private security officers doing law enforcement duties will be treated as public servants under the amended definition.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: With the amendments to the definition of "public servant" to include persons who are employed by contractors engaged to perform certain duties on behalf of the Government or a Statutory Board, such as law enforcement functions and escorting persons in remand and prisoners, I wish to ask the Minister to clarify whether private security officers who are not Auxiliary Police Officers will be treated as "public servants" if they are engaged to carry out law enforcement duties, such as crowd control and access control, including issuing of summonses for offences and other law enforcement duties.

sections.label: Public legal education materials
sections.summary: The Ministry should partner agencies and stakeholders to produce easy-to-read materials so the public, victims and would-be perpetrators know the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The Ministry should partner the various agencies and stakeholders to produce suitable reading, reference material, or simple pocket guides in easy to read and comprehend format, so that the public and potential victims will know the law has better protected them, and would-be perpetrators will know that the law has caught up with them.

sections.label: Repeal of marital rape immunity
sections.summary: The passage states that marriage no longer implies automatic consent to sexual relations and that the Bill rightly repeals marital rape immunity.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We no longer believe today that marriage implies the automatic consent of a spouse to sexual relations.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is right that this Bill repeals the marital rape immunity.

sections.label: Protection for vulnerable adults
sections.summary: The Bill expands protection for vulnerable adults, making neglect and abuse causing death serious offences and giving household members a duty of care.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This is important because in our ageing society, the number of vulnerable elderly will increase significantly in the coming years.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is right that the Bill expands protection for such vulnerable adults by making it clear, in the new section 304B of the Penal Code, that neglect and abuse leading to the death of a vulnerable adult are serious offences.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Section 304C further provides that persons in the same household have a duty of care to stop such neglect or abuse.

sections.label: Decriminalising attempted suicide, abetting suicide
sections.summary: The member agrees with decriminalising attempted suicide but says society is rightfully more cautious about abetting suicide, which is euthanasia in practice.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: While I agree with this Bill's proposal to decriminalise attempted suicide, I think society is rightfully more cautious on the matter of abetting suicide, which is what euthanasia is in practice.

sections.label: Standard of care at end of life
sections.summary: A landmark case set the standard of care needed to avoid a neglect charge at the end of life, with possible severe impact.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A landmark case that determined the particular standard of care required, to avoid the charge of neglect at the end of life, could have severe impact on the practice of medicine and the rights of families and the vulnerable elderly.

sections.label: Expanded protection from sexual offences
sections.summary: The Bill expands protection from sexual offences, removing the limited marital immunity defence for rape and adding provisions on consent, voyeurism, sexual exposure and child abuse.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Next, my concern on the social standards that give the law effect are centred on this Bill’s expanded protection from sexual offences.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: These revisions, include removal of the limited marital immunity defence for rape in section 375 of the Penal Code and substantive new provisions in sections 376 and 377 on consent, voyeurism, sexual exposure and child abuse.

sections.label: Monica Baey voyeurism case
sections.summary: Ms Monica Baey highlighted her experience as a voyeurism victim, showing inadequacies in how her institution handles sexual misconduct cases.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Ms Monica Baey has bravely highlighted her own experience as a victim of voyeurism, which has shown inadequacies in how her institution handles sexual misconduct cases.

sections.label: Understanding sexual offences incidence
sections.summary: Correcting this must start with understanding the actual incidence of sexual offences and harassment and the social conditions normalising them.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Serious efforts to correct this must start with attempting to understand the actual incidence of sexual offences and harassment in Singapore, the social conditions around the normalisation and perpetration of such offences amongst some social circles and applying the right educational and policy levers to correct those social conditions.

sections.label: Indian Penal Code in Singapore
sections.summary: A decade later, substantially the same Indian Penal Code with its 511 sections was enacted in Singapore through Ordinance 4 of 1871.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: A decade later, substantially the same copy of the Indian Penal Code with its 511 sections was enacted as law in Singapore through Ordinance 4 of 1871 when Singapore was part of the Straits Settlement.

sections.label: Breadth of Penal Code review
sections.summary: The Bill shows the review's breadth: extraterritorial jurisdiction, fault and physical elements, defences, new offences, sentences, and removing anachronistic offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: A simple perusal of the Bill will reveal the extraordinary breadth of the review that was undertaken.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We see updates in the following areas: (a) the extraterritorial criminal jurisdiction of the offences; (b) concepts of fault and physical elements that usually make up an offence; these elements are the equivalent of the "computer source codes" of the criminal provisions; (c) general defences that may be raised by accused persons; (d) creation of new offences and enhancement of sentences to protect the vulnerable and minors and to deal with modern circumstances and advances in technology; (e) updating of sentences to ensure their deterrent effect; and (f) removing offences which are seen as anachronistic or irrelevant.

sections.label: Removal of thought crime provisions
sections.summary: The Minister accepted a suggestion to remove Penal Code sections 121A and 121B, which criminalised imagining harm to the President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: First, I am glad that the hon Minister, through a notice of amendment issued on 26 April 2019, accepted my suggestion made outside this House after the First Reading of this Bill to remove the thought crime provisions, namely, sections 121A and 121B in the Penal Code.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Presently, it is an offence to imagine the death, hurt, imprisonment or restraint of the President, and the accused, if convicted, may be sentenced to death or imprisonment for life.

sections.label: Narrower criminal conspiracy provision
sections.summary: Proposed section 120A is narrower and would decriminalise conspiracy to commit an illegal act defined as grounds for civil action.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Second, I note that the proposed section 120A dealing with "criminal conspiracy" is significantly narrower.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The proposed provision would have the effect of decriminalising a conspiracy to commit an illegal act, which was defined as anything that furnishes ground for a civil action.

sections.label: Abolishing section 309 suicide attempt
sections.summary: The speaker has misgivings about abolishing section 309, noting it currently allows mandatory treatment orders instead of jail.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Third, I have misgivings, just like the hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza, on the proposal to abolish section 309 of the Penal Code which currently criminalises an attempt to commit suicide.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I appreciate the point made by Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin as well as the PCRC that "persons who commit such offences should undergo treatment instead".

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I wish to point out though that section 309 of the Penal Code, read with the CPC, now allows the Court to impose on persons convicted for the offence of attempting suicide, mandatory treatment orders aimed at providing psychiatric treatment for such persons in lieu of the jail term provided in the Penal Code.

sections.label: Outcome of the Bill
sections.summary: The Bill is relevant, practical and well-calibrated, repealing marital immunity for rape and raising penalties for offences against vulnerable victims.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The outcome of the Bill is one that is relevant, practical and well-calibrated to ensure that the vulnerable are protected, and the resulting punishments accurately reflect moral culpability.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am very heartened to hear that the latest changes repeal marital immunity for rape and introduce higher penalties for offences knowingly committed against vulnerable victims.

sections.label: Increased child abuse reporting
sections.summary: Efforts led to enhanced detection, reporting and management of child abuse cases, with a 60% increase in reporting.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Their endeavours have led to enhanced detection, reporting and management of child abuse cases, resulting in a very significant increase of 60% in reporting.

sections.label: Domestic violence cases and hotline
sections.summary: A PAVE study found abused spouses were 72% of new cases; the speaker requests a central dedicated domestic violence hotline.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A study by the organisation PAVE, based on 3,600 cases over the last 10 years, found that victims who are physically or psychologically abused by their spouse made up a disquieting 72% of new cases.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the interest of reducing prolonged cases of domestic violence and abuse, I request that a central dedicated hotline be set up with trained personnel to handle all domestic violence calls.

sections.label: Domestic violence evidence apps
sections.summary: Free apps like Smartsafe and Bright Sky help women collect evidence such as photographs, videos and recordings, saved off device for court use.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Smartsafe app, by the Domestic Violence Resource Centre in Australia or the Bright Sky app by the UK charity body are a few examples.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: These free apps help women collect detailed evidence in order to obtain a protection order or prove a breach of one.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: They collect photographs, videos and recordings and save them off device to ensure that the evidence is protected and can be used in court later when victims are ready to lodge a report.

sections.label: App features for abuse victims
sections.summary: An app with discreet evidence gathering, a one-touch Police alert and the central hotline number would benefit domestic abuse victims in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: To recap and emphasise, an app mentioned above would greatly benefit victims of domestic abuse and facilitate the ease of reporting for abuse cases.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: By adding features, such as discreet evidence gathering, a one-touch Police alert option and the central hotline number, we can ensure that every service is synergised to provide the best protection and survivor-centric help to all victims of domestic violence in Singapore.

sections.label: Proposed section 304C scope
sections.summary: The proposed section 304C would apply to the person who committed the unlawful act and to a witness who did nothing to stop the abuse.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The new provision proposed in section 304C would apply to both the person who committed the unlawful act as well as to someone who witnessed the abuse but stood by and did nothing to stop the abuse.

sections.label: Considering circumstances before prosecution
sections.summary: The speaker says she would have been liable under proposed section 304C and urges considering circumstances and mental state before prosecution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: She would have been liable under the new proposed section 304C.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: I would, therefore, urge that we consider such circumstances and the mental state of the individuals before we consider prosecution.

sections.label: Rise in BPC cases
sections.summary: Cases rose from 71 in 2016 to 108 in 2018, with BPC cases for ages 11-12 and 13-14 also increasing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The number of cases has risen from 71 in 2016, to 108 in 2018.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Statistics from MSF show that for those between 11 and 12 years old, the number of BPC cases increased almost three-fold from three in 2016 to eight in 2018, while those in the age band of 13-14 years old saw an increase of more than two-fold, from 24 cases in 2016, to 56 cases in 2018.

sections.label: Cases brought to Courts
sections.summary: A September 2018 Straits Times report said at least five such cases were brought to the Courts between 2016 and 2017, versus seven between 2000 and 2011.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: According to a report by the Straits Times in September 2018, at least five such cases were brought to the Courts between 2016 and 2017, compared to seven cases between 2000 and 2011.

sections.label: Abuse death prosecution limits
sections.summary: AGC explained the circumstances of a death and the law's limits, so abusers in series-of-acts cases are likely prosecuted for grievous hurt, punishable by up to 10 years' jail, fine and caning.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: At that time, AGC explained the specific circumstances which led to her unfortunate death and the limitations of the law which requires evidence that the abuser had the intention to cause death or fatal injury.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Therefore, in cases where the abuse consists of a series of acts that eventually lead to death, the abuser is likely to be prosecuted under the crime of causing grievous hurt, which carries a penalty of up to 10 years' jail, with possible fine and caning.

sections.label: Penalty amendments and Vulnerable Adults Act
sections.summary: The amendments address penalty concerns and may deter such conduct, and the speaker seeks clarification on how the Bill's clauses relate to the Vulnerable Adults Act.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The amendments proposed today address the other concerns about penalties and hopefully forms a deterrent against such heinous conduct.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I would like though to seek a clarification about how the proposed clauses in this Bill would sit vis-a-vis the terms in the Vulnerable Adults Act.

sections.label: Liability scope and household abuse
sections.summary: The speaker asks the rationale for differing liability scope and cautions against prosecuting household members who lack power to stop abuse, noting the offence requires failure to take reasonable protective steps.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: What is the rationale for the difference in the scope of liability in these provisions?

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I also note that in criminalising the offence of causing or allowing the death of child under 14 years of age or vulnerable person in the same household, we need to be cautious not to prosecute those who are in the same household but may not have the power to stop the abuse as they themselves may be suffering from the abuse.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I note that the offence will only be made out if there is a failure to take reasonable steps to protect the victims.

sections.label: Rape definition and male victims
sections.summary: The Court recognised section 376's gender neutrality, and the speaker is heartened that PCRC proposed amending sections 375 and 376 so rape includes non-consensual penetration and men can be victims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: While the Court has recognised the gender neutrality of section 376 as it stood at that time, I am heartened that the PCRC has also proposed amendments to sections 375 and 376, so that the definition of "rape" would include non-consensual penetration and that men can be victims of rape as well.

sections.label: Child abuse material offences and penalties
sections.summary: The new section criminalises non-fictional and indistinguishable fictional child abuse material, with penalties of up to 10, seven and five years' imprisonment plus fine and caning for production, distribution or sale, and advertising or seeking.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: The new section criminalises non-fictional child abuse as well as fictional child abuse material where it is indistinguishable if the child portrayed is real or fictional.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: The punishments are hefty, and rightfully so: a term of imprisonment which may extend to 10 years, and liable to fine and to caning for using or involving a child in the production of child abuse or producing child abuse material under 377BG (2) and 377BH (2); the term of imprisonment which may extend to seven years, and liable to fine and to caning for distributing or selling child abuse material as well as a term of imprisonment which may extend to five years, and liable to fine and to caning for advertising or seeking child abuse material.

sections.label: Criminalising fantasy child abuse material
sections.summary: The speaker says any material should be considered equally abhorrent for its intent and asks the Ministry to consider criminalising all fantasy or virtual child abuse material, termed non-photographic pornographic images of children.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: As such, any material, in any form, should be considered equally abhorrent for its intent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Therefore, I ask that the Ministry consider including the criminalising of all fantasy or virtual child abuse material, which is what is usually termed as non-photographic pornographic images of children (NPPIC).

sections.label: Criminalising all child abuse material
sections.summary: A Member urges criminalising all child abuse material including NPPIC, citing research and the Minister's Second Reading speech, while supporting the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: His research shows those addicted to pornographic materials will want and will seek more explicit or extreme material and likely end up desiring to act out what they have seen.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Minister Shanmugam also spoke in his speech for the Second Reading of this Bill that the inclusion of materials which are indistinguishable whether the child portrayed is fictional or non-fictional is to remove the defence by any accused that the material that he or she has been caught with is fictional.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Therefore, should it not be the case that all child abuse material in whatever form it takes should be criminalised?

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: I, therefore, believe there is fertile ground to include all child abuse material as I have described because technology will make it ever harder to distinguish real and virtual as well as the psychological correlation progressing from virtual to real consumption Although I believe that the amendments to the Penal Code as proposed under the Criminal Law Reform Bill are much needed and have been robustly discussed, I ask that my proposal to criminalise all forms of child abuse material, including NPPIC, be considered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding my comments and proposal, I support the Bill.

sections.label: Singapore suicide statistics
sections.summary: WHO data ranks Singapore 62nd of 176 countries, with about 10 suicides per 100,000 and 361 suicides in 2017.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: According to WHO, Singapore ranked 62 out of 176 countries with a suicide rate of almost 10 suicides per 100,000 people.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: This also means that Singapore has 2.5 times more deaths from suicide than transport accidents in 2017, when 361 people killed themselves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: The number of elderly aged above 60 who took their own lives also reached an all-time high in 2017, at 129 suicides.

sections.label: Suicide leading cause of youth deaths
sections.summary: Suicide is the leading cause of death for those aged between 10 and 29 in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Suicide is the leading cause of death for those aged between 10 and 29 in Singapore.

sections.label: Taxi drivers beaten by passengers
sections.summary: In 2018, 40 taxi drivers were beaten by passengers, but only four cases were prosecuted in Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: (In Mandarin):   In 2018, there were 40 taxi drivers who were beaten up by their passengers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: The Police did not necessarily investigate unless the victim spent money and time to go to the Magistrate's Court to raise a complaint.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: So, out of these 40 incidents, only four cases were finally prosecuted in Court.

sections.label: Proactive police investigation of VCH
sections.summary: A Member suggests the Police proactively investigate VCH incidents in certain circumstances even without grievous hurt, as current process seems unfair to victims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: All these take time and money, so it does not appear to be fair to the victims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Therefore, I would like to suggest to the Minister that the Police should proactively investigate incidences of "VCH" under certain circumstances, even though the victim was not deemed to have suffered grievous hurt.

sections.label: Safeguards against false allegations
sections.summary: A Member asks what additional Police safeguards, beyond enhanced punishment for false statements, will prevent and deter false allegations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
sentences.text: While it is morally right to protect women from abusive husbands who force themselves on their wives, I would like to ask the Minister what additional safeguards, besides enhancing the punishment of providing false statement, if any, the Police will take to prevent and deter such false allegations.

sections.label: Investigating pre-law voyeuristic videos
sections.summary: Asks whether cases can be investigated and site owners compelled to remove voyeuristic videos distributed before the law but still online after.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: At the same time, can I clarify with the Minister that victims can still have their cases investigated if the videos were distributed prior to the passing of the law but still found on different websites after the passing of this law?

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Would the Police have the powers to compel the owners of these sites to remove such voyeuristic materials?

sections.label: Sections 424A and 424B introduced
sections.summary: MHA introduced sections 424A and 424B to tackle situations like the London Whale case and LIBOR manipulation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Specifically, MHA has introduced section 424A and section 424B to tackle situations, such as the London Whale case involving J P Morgan or the Manipulation of the LIBOR in 2012 involving multiple banks.

sections.label: Penalty under new section 424A
sections.summary: The new section 424A carries imprisonment of up to 20 years, twice as heavy as the current section 420 cheating offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Under the new section 424A, the penalty of imprisonment up to 20 years is twice as heavy as the current section 420 offence of cheating.

sections.label: Stakeholder engagement and written feedback
sections.summary: More than 700 stakeholders joined engagement sessions and over 60 individuals and organisations gave written feedback.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: More than 700 stakeholders participated in the engagement sessions and more than 60 individuals and organisations provided written feedback.

sections.label: Abolishing attempted suicide offence
sections.summary: The Bill takes the progressive step of abolishing the offence of attempted suicide.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Next, the Bill takes the progressive step of abolishing the offence of attempted suicide.

sections.label: Repealing marital immunity for rape
sections.summary: The Bill repeals marital immunity for rape, which had been supported by the public and religious, legal and social sectors.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Next, the Bill repeals the marital immunity for rape, something which I and many Members of this House have spoken up on and which had been strongly supported by members of the public and representatives from the religious, legal and social sectors during the public consultation process.

sections.label: Minimum Age of Criminal Responsibility raised
sections.summary: The Minimum Age of Criminal Responsibility is raised from seven to 10, so children below that age are considered incapable of crime.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: One other positive aspect I would like to highlight is the raising of the Minimum Age of Criminal Responsibility (MACR) from seven to 10, where children below this threshold are considered incapable of crime.

sections.label: Call for age 12 standard
sections.summary: The change matches England and Hong Kong, but the speaker believes Singapore could set a precedent by meeting the international standard of 12 years old.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: While this change puts us on par with the laws in England and Hong Kong, Sir, I believe that Singapore could benefit from setting a positive precedent for other countries by meeting the internationally acceptable standard or level of 12 years old.

sections.label: Greater penalties for offences against vulnerable persons
sections.summary: The Bill provides greater penalties for offences against domestic workers, vulnerable persons, persons below 14, and people in intimate or close relationships.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: In relation to vulnerable persons, this Bill makes provision for greater penalties for offences against the following: domestic workers, vulnerable persons, persons below 14 years, people in intimate relationships, people in close relationships, and "intimate relationships" refers to partners, sexual or not, and "close relationships" include the broader family.

sections.label: Marital immunity to rape abolished
sections.summary: The marital immunity to rape has been abolished in a different part of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: On a related note, though in a different part of the Bill, the marital immunity to rape has also been abolished.

sections.label: Internet-age crimes and child pornography
sections.summary: The Bill changes the Code for Internet-age crimes including voyeurism, intimate photos or videos, and a wide range of child pornography offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I also welcome the changes to the Code in relation to crimes that have become particularly damaging in the Internet age.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: These include specific offences in relation to voyeurism, the taking of intimate photos or videos of a person without their knowledge, possession of the same, or even gaining access to it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Child pornography is another area that receives special legislative attention, with a wide range of offences covering those who exploit children to provide the material, those who profit from it or distribute it and those who access it.

sections.label: VAA intrusive powers
sections.summary: The VAA gives the state powers to take intrusive measures, such as removing a vulnerable adult from their living conditions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The VAA provides powers to the state to take intrusive measures, such as removal of the vulnerable adult from their living conditions.

sections.label: PCRC on vulnerable persons definition
sections.summary: PCRC viewed the VAA definition as too narrow for the Penal Code and recommended a wider definition of vulnerable persons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: PCRC was of the view that the definition in the VAA was too narrow for the purposes of the Penal Code, and it recommended for "vulnerable persons" in the Penal Code to be wider to cover more persons.

sections.label: Defence under section 304C
sections.summary: A person is not guilty under section 304C if she could not have been expected in her circumstances to protect the victim.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The provision provides that a person is not guilty of an offence under section 304C if she could not have been expected in her circumstances to take steps to protect the victim from the significant risk of grievous hurt.

sections.label: Vulnerability and enhanced punishment
sections.summary: If the vulnerability did not make the person more susceptible to the offence, the offender gets punishment but not enhanced punishment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: If the vulnerability did not make the person more susceptible to the offence, the offender will be subjected to punishment but not enhanced punishment.

sections.label: Maximum penalty enhancement
sections.summary: The current maximum penalty of three months will be enhanced to two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The current maximum penalty is three months and it will be enhanced to two years.

sections.label: Increased imprisonment terms for child offences
sections.summary: Where death is caused, the maximum imprisonment term increased from seven to 14 years; where death is not caused, from four to eight years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: Where death is caused to the child or young person, the maximum imprisonment term has been increased from seven to 14 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: Where death is not caused, the maximum imprisonment term has been increased from four to eight years.

sections.label: Non-consensual sex with spouse
sections.summary: The answer is that all non-consensual sex with one's spouse will be an offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The answer is all non-consensual sex with one’s spouse will be an offence.

sections.label: Legal age of marriage
sections.summary: The legal age of marriage is 18, though minors may marry with special approval, which is rare and safeguarded.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The legal age of marriage is set at 18 years of age.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: We allow minors in Singapore to enter into marriage with special approval, but these marriages are extremely rare and robust safeguards are in place.

sections.label: Amendments increase maximum punishment
sections.summary: The amendments multiply the maximum punishment by 10 times to 10 years' imprisonment, and for certain other categories.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The amendments multiply the maximum punishment by 10 times to 10 years’ imprisonment, and for certain other categories.

sections.label: Safeguards after decriminalisation
sections.summary: Police and Singapore Civil Defence Force intervention safeguards will remain after decriminalisation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The safeguards that were previously there – Police intervention, Singapore Civil Defence Force intervention – will still be there, post-decriminalisation.

sections.label: Average annual reports number
sections.summary: The number has been steady in the last five years, with an average annual number of reports of 1,210.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The number has been steady in the last five years, and the average annual number of reports is 1,210.

sections.label: Raising MACR to 10
sections.summary: After looking at factors such as criminal activity among age groups, it was assessed that raising the MACR to 10 years would not significantly threaten public safety.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: So, we looked at factors, such as prevailing criminal activity among the various age groups.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: We assessed that there would not be a significant threat to public safety to raise the MACR to 10 years of age.

sections.label: Arrestable offences against children
sections.summary: All Penal Code offences against children under 14, vulnerable persons and domestic workers will be arrestable regardless of the underlying offence's arrestability.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: All Penal Code offences committed against children under 14, vulnerable persons and domestic workers will be made arrestable, regardless of the arrestability of the underlying offence.

sections.label: New fraud offence victim requirement
sections.summary: The new offence of fraud does not require an identifiable victim.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The new offence of fraud does not require an identifiable victim.

sections.label: Proposed fraud offence details
sections.summary: The proposed fraud offence is adapted from the UK Fraud Act 2006, carries a heavier maximum punishment of 20 years' imprisonment, and focuses on the offender's culpability.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The proposed fraud offence is adapted from the UK Fraud Act 2006.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: It has a heavier maximum punishment – 20 years’ imprisonment, as opposed to 10 years in the UK – to account for the fact that a single count of fraud can encompass a single deceptive scheme which affects multiple victims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The higher maximum punishment is to ensure that complex, large-scale frauds receive the appropriate sentence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The purpose of the new fraud offence is to focus on the culpability of the offender and not the effect it may have had on the victim.

sections.label: Presumptive minimum sentence amendments
sections.summary: The amendments set out the provisions to which presumptive minimum sentences apply, including certain offences under the Passport Act, Fisheries Act and Immigration Act, and the list is tightly scoped.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The amendments set out the provisions which presumptive minimum sentences apply to.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: They include provisions in laws outside the Penal Code, including certain offences under the Passport Act, the Fisheries Act and the Immigration Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The list of offences presumptive minimum sentences will be applied to is tightly scoped.

sections.label: Protection for public servants
sections.summary: Under the provision, whether they are covered and entitled to protection as public servants depends on the functions they perform.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: Under the provision, it would depend on the functions that they perform.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: So, if they perform a function as set out in the Bill, yes, they will be covered and they will be entitled to the protection accorded to public servants.

sections.label: Amendment to section 121A
sections.summary: The intent behind the amendment to section 121A is to remove the limbs of the offence that do not require any physical act or omission.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The intent behind the amendment to section 121A is to remove the limbs of the offence that do not require the offender to commit any physical act or omission.

sections.label: Death penalty removed, imprisonment option
sections.summary: The death penalty will be removed as a punishment option for this offence, and imprisonment of up to 20 years will be included as a sentencing option.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The death penalty will also be removed as a punishment option for this offence, and an imprisonment sentence of up to 20 years will be included as a sentencing option.

sections.label: Section 121B thought crime limbs
sections.summary: The amendments delete the words "compasses, imagines, invents, devises or intends" from section 121B and replace them with "plans".

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The amendments to section 121B remove the “thought crime” limbs of the offence, by deleting the words “compasses, imagines, invents, devises or intends”, and replacing them with the modern term of “plans”.

sections.label: Death penalty removed for offence
sections.summary: The death penalty is removed as a punishment for this offence, and imprisonment of up to 20 years is included as a sentencing option.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The death penalty will also be removed as a punishment option for this offence, and an imprisonment sentence of up to 20 years will be included as a sentencing option.

sections.label: Scope of new death offences
sections.summary: Amendments 1 to 4 set the offender scope for "causing death by sustained abuse", and Amendments 5 to 9 include domestic workers as victims of "causing or allowing death".

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: Amendments 1 to 4 provide that the scope of offenders covered by the new offence of "causing death by sustained abuse" should cover persons who have care, custody and control of a child or a vulnerable person, or an employer of the domestic worker, member of the employer's household, or the employment agent of a domestic worker.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: Amendments 5 to 9 provide that the scope of victims covered by the new offence of "causing or allowing death" includes domestic workers.

sections.label: Editorial amendments to offence provisions
sections.summary: The amendment makes editorial amendments to section 377D, to "representation" definitions in sections 424A and 424B, and on attempt offences and mandatory minimum sentences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The amendment makes editorial amendments to the list of minor-specific offences in section 377D.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The amendment makes editorial amendments to ensure that similar definitions of “representation” apply for the offences of fraud introduced in sections 424A and 424B.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The amendments are editorial amendments to provide clear examples of situations where a person has committed an offence of attempt, and to provide that for offences of attempts, mandatory minimum sentences for the underlying offence do not apply.

sections.label: Lifting marital privilege situations
sections.summary: The amendments apply the lifting of marital privilege under section 124 of the Evidence Act to child abuse offences against persons below 16 and all hurt offences against children.

sentences.speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
sentences.text: The amendments provide that the lifting of marital privilege under section 124 of the Evidence Act will apply to the following situations: (a)	Child abuse offences committed against a person below 16 years old; (b)	All hurt offences committed against children.
